contracts.contract_plain_english: For the power-of-two divide-and-conquer solver SylR applied to the nonsingular ordinary equation AR−RB=−C, the error at size n is the sum of an amplified four-subproblem error and a forcing term from right-hand-side rounding and matrix multiplication. Solving that recurrence gives equation (20), with polynomial factors in n and μ(n/2) and the Sylvester condition ratio raised to 1+log2 n; comparison with the conventional forward-error bound yields the paper's logarithmic-stability conclusion. (PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: affine recurrence, equation (20), and following sentence).

source_evidence.observation: The ordinary problem is A R − R B = −C. When A and B are upper triangular, the associated triangular system is nonsingular precisely when their eigenvalues are distinct.

source_evidence.anchor: equations (14)–(18) and paragraph introducing the recursive algorithm
source_evidence.observation: The matrices are split conformally into 2-by-2 blocks, producing four smaller Sylvester equations solved in the order R21, then R11 and R22, then R12; for simplicity all matrices are assumed square, of the same power-of-two dimension.
SylR takes n-by-n A, B, C, uses the scalar base case R = −C/(A−B), and recursively constructs R21, R11, R22, and R12 with matrix products in their right-hand sides.
The paper defines sep(A,B) = σmin(I⊗A−B^T⊗I) = min_{||R||F=1}||AR−RB||F and states sep(Aii,Bjj) ≥ sep(A,B) for every recursive subproblem.
err(n′) bounds the error in any smaller Sylvester solution of dimension n′ encountered by the algorithm, including errors in computing its right-hand side.
A right-hand-side perturbation bounded in norm by x can change the solution in norm by x/sep(A,B), and the proof also uses the product-error rule (8).

source_evidence.anchor: first asymptotic line following the affine recurrence
source_evidence.observation: The recurrence is bounded by O((nε/sep(A,B))(||C||+μ(n/2)(||A||+||B||)||R||)(2+(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^(log2 n)).
The final displayed bound is O(n^(1+log2 3) μ(n/2) ε ||R|| ((||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^(1+log2 n)).
The paper compares equation (20) with the conventional bound O(ε||R||(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B)) and concludes that SylR is logarithmically stable.
Logarithmic stability is defined by a relative error of the form O(ε)κf(x)^χ(n) + O(ε²), where χ(n) is at least 1 and is bounded by a polynomial in log n.

statement.algorithm_linkage: The recurrence and equation (20) belong specifically to the divide-and-conquer ordinary Sylvester solver SylR: it recursively forms right-hand sides with fast matrix multiplication, solves four n/2 subproblems, and uses the global lower bound sep(Aii,Bjj) ≥ sep(A,B) to control error amplification. They are not a proved recurrence for the generalized two-equation variant, which the paper only sketches afterward. (PDF p. 26, printed p. 84, anchor: equations (14)–(18); PDF p. 27, printed p. 85, anchor: SylR and equation (19); PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: equation (20) and following generalized-case paragraph).
binders: n is a positive power of 2 for the equal-halving recursive SylR analysis. (PDF p. 26, printed p. 84, anchor: paragraph before SylR; PDF p. 27, printed p. 85, anchor: complexity-analysis assumption).

A, B, and C are n-by-n matrices; A and B are upper triangular in the Schur-form setting. (PDF p. 26, printed p. 84, anchor: Sylvester-equation discussion; PDF p. 27, printed p. 85, anchor: SylR header).

R is the exact solution of A R − R B = −C against which the computed recursive result is compared. (PDF p. 26, printed p. 84, anchor: ordinary Sylvester equation; PDF p. 27, printed p. 85, anchor: err induction hypothesis).

ε is machine epsilon, μ(n/2) is the multiplication-error factor at half dimension, and err(n) is a recursive absolute-error bound. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 60, anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 27, printed p. 85, anchor: induction hypothesis; PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: affine recurrence).
conclusions: The affine error recurrence is err(n) = (4 + 2(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))err(n/2) + (ε/sep(A,B))(3||C|| + 2μ(n/2)(||A||+||B||)||R||). (PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: recurrence immediately before equation (20)).

Its first displayed asymptotic solution is err(n) ≤ O((nε/sep(A,B))(||C|| + μ(n/2)(||A||+||B||)||R||)(2 + (||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^(log2 n)). (PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: first asymptotic line following the recurrence).
The further simplified bound is err(n) ≤ O(n^(1+log2 3) μ(n/2) ε ||R|| ((||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B))^(1+log2 n)). (PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: equation (20)).

Because a conventional Sylvester solver has error O(ε||R||(||A||+||B||)/sep(A,B)), the paper concludes that recursive SylR is logarithmically stable. (PDF p. 28, printed p. 86, anchor: sentence following equation (20)).
